newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece aims to meet Maastricht by '98-end - minister.
newsitem.headline: Greece aims to meet Maastricht by '98-end - minister.

text.p: Greece is striving to meet its EU economic convergence criteria by the end of 1998 so that it can join the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on an equal basis, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou said in an interview.
"The convergence programme ends in two years. And 1998 is our reference point," he was quoted as saying in the interview with the weekly "Ekonomikos Tahydromos."
"My goal is for Greece to satisfy the Maastricht criteria in 1998 so that it can seek participation in the EMU on an equal basis in the following two years," he said.
The run-up to 1998 will be "critical for the Greek economy," he said, adding he was determined to stop major tax evaders and bring in significant new revenues.
"There must be greater emphasis given to major tax evasion, which is not only socially provocative and unacceptable but...can bring significant revenues," he said.
Papandoniou, who took over the finance ministry after the socialist party won the national election last month, has said he will submit a draft tax bill in parliament soon.

"We do not rule out making small changes in the tax system to make it fairer and more effective...(but) I believe that tax checks should turn primarily towards big business because that is where there is the greatest tax evasion," he said. Nightclubs and bars would also be targeted.
Echoing a recent policy speech by Prime Minister Costas Simitis, he said the wealthy would be taxed harder, but taxing property was difficult because of the absence of a land register.
"The tax pressure on high income earners will increase, and a significant increase in the wealth indicators in the consumption of luxury items will help in this," he said.
Papandoniou said correcting structural problems would be a long-term effort in sectors such as agriculture, tourism and small- and medium-size enterprises.
"Even after the completion of convergence, there will remain certain important structural problems which will differentiate us from the rest of the European Union," he said.
He said he had brought up defence spending at a recent informal ECOFIN council meeting, which groups EU economy and finance ministers, and Greece's position had been met with "understanding".

The Greek military is pushing for a $10 billion arms package over the next five years, but a number of senior officials have said such a large sum would cripple Greece's efforts to meet the Maastricht criteria.

Papandoniou said Simitis would raise the defence spending issue at a coming EU summit. Greece spends a higher percent of GDP on arms than any other NATO country, citing its tense relations with neighbouring Turkey. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
